title: A Priori Power Analysis for t-tests, ANOVA, and Regression

content.quick: Statistical power (1 - beta = 0.80) is the probability of correctly detecting a real effect when one exists. Using G*Power 3.1 before data collection (a priori) ensures your thesis has adequate sample size to avoid false-negative Type II errors.

sentences.text: Statistical power represents the probability that a statistical test will correctly reject a false null hypothesis.
sentences.simple: Statistical power means the chance that your test will successfully find a real effect if it actually exists in the real world.
sentences.plain: Statistical power represents the probability that a statistical test will correctly reject a false null hypothesis.
sentences.technical: Statistical power ($1 - \beta$) quantifies the operational probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis under specified alternative parameterizations.

data.meaning: The likelihood of finding a statistically significant result when a true effect actually exists in the target population.
data.example: At 80% power, you have an 80% chance of detecting a significant correlation and a 20% risk of missing it (Type II error).

blocks.explain: Think of statistical power like the zoom lens on a telescope. If your sample size is tiny, your lens is blurry, and you will miss real stars (Type II error). An 80% power level means your lens is sharp enough to detect real relationships 4 times out of 5.

questions.q: What does a statistical power level of 0.80 (80%) mean in an empirical research thesis?
options: There is an 80% chance that your data contains zero errors.
There is an 80% probability of detecting a statistically significant effect if a true effect exists in the population.
80% of your participants will return completed questionnaires.
The null hypothesis has an 80% probability of being true.
questions.explanation: Statistical power (1 - beta) is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. At power = 0.80, you have an 80% chance of successfully finding a real effect and a 20% risk of missing it (Type II error).

visual.title: Effect Size

data.meaning: A quantitative reflection of the magnitude of an experimental treatment or the strength of a relationship between two variables.
data.example: Cohen's d = 0.50 means the treatment group scored half a standard deviation higher than the control group.

visual.caption: Unlike p-values, effect size tells you the practical significance of a finding.

sentences.text: Jacob Cohen established universal benchmark values for small, medium, and large effect sizes across different statistical procedures.
sentences.simple: Famous statistician Jacob Cohen gave standard numbers for small, medium, and large effects for every common statistical test.
sentences.plain: Jacob Cohen established universal benchmark values for small, medium, and large effect sizes across different statistical procedures.
sentences.technical: Cohen's (1988) seminal taxonomy operationalized standardized effect size metrics, classifying deviations into small, medium, and large thresholds.

visual.title: Cohen's Effect Size Benchmarks Master Table
visual.caption: When no prior study exists, researchers conventionally assume a medium effect size.

sentences.text: In multiple linear regression, effect size is measured using Cohen's f-squared, which is derived directly from the expected R-squared value.
sentences.simple: In regression analysis, effect size is called f², and it comes directly from how much variance (R²) your model explains.
sentences.plain: In multiple linear regression, effect size is measured using Cohen's f-squared, which is derived directly from the expected R-squared value.
sentences.technical: In multivariable regression architectures, the omnibus effect size metric $f^2$ is computed as the ratio: $f^2 = R^2 / (1 - R^2)$.

sentences.text: Smaller anticipated effects require substantially larger sample sizes to reach statistical significance.
sentences.simple: If the effect you are looking for is tiny and subtle, you need a much bigger sample size to prove it is real.
sentences.plain: Smaller anticipated effects require substantially larger sample sizes to reach statistical significance.
sentences.technical: Required sample size scales inversely with effect magnitude: detecting subtle population deviations necessitates proportionally expansive sample registries.

blocks.explain: If you are looking for a loud noise (large effect), you only need a few people to hear it. If you are listening for a faint whisper (small effect), you need hundreds of participants. For an MS thesis, assuming a 'medium effect' is the safe, standard middle ground accepted by all Pakistani universities.

questions.q: What is the standard Cohen's benchmark value for a medium effect size (f²) in multiple linear regression?
questions.hint: Check the Cohen benchmarks master table above for multiple regression.
questions.explanation: In multiple regression, Cohen (1988) defined f² = 0.02 as small, f² = 0.15 as medium, and f² = 0.35 as large. (Note: d = 0.50 is the medium benchmark for t-tests, not regression f²).

blocks.explain: G*Power gives you the mathematical minimum. If G*Power says you need 92 people, never distribute exactly 92 surveys! People will spill tea on them, leave pages blank, or refuse to return them. Hand out 120 or 130 surveys so that after cleaning the data, you still have at least 92 pristine responses.

sentences.text: A widespread error among students is conducting post-hoc power calculations after their study fails to find significant results.
sentences.simple: A big mistake students make is running G*Power after their experiment fails, trying to make an excuse for why it didn't work.
sentences.plain: A widespread error among students is conducting post-hoc power calculations after their study fails to find significant results.
sentences.technical: A pervasive methodological fallacy involves calculating observed (post-hoc) power retrospectively following nonsignificant statistical outcomes.

visual.title: A Priori vs Post-Hoc Power Fallacy

data.mistake: Running G*Power after data collection: 'Our p = .12 because post-hoc power was only 40%.'
data.why: Observed post-hoc power is merely a 1-to-1 mathematical transformation of the p-value; it adds zero new empirical information.
data.fix: Always conduct A Priori power analysis before collecting data, and report confidence intervals for non-significant findings.

visual.caption: Leading statisticians (Hoenig & Heisey, 2001) condemn post-hoc power as mathematically circular.

sentences.text: Statisticians have proven that observed post-hoc power is merely a redundant mathematical transformation of the p-value and provides zero explanatory value.
sentences.simple: Statisticians proved that checking power after your test is finished tells you nothing new; it just repeats your p-value in a different shape.
sentences.plain: Statisticians have proven that observed post-hoc power is merely a redundant mathematical transformation of the p-value and provides zero explanatory value.
sentences.technical: Mathematical proofs demonstrate that retrospective power is confounded with the test statistic, yielding an entirely circular and tautological diagnostic.

visual.title: The Post-Hoc Power Fallacy

data.text: Calculating power after finding a non-significant result is like checking the weather forecast for yesterday to see if it rained.
data.author: Prof. Andy Field (Discovering Statistics)

visual.caption: Power analysis belongs strictly in the research design phase.

blocks.explain: Never wait until your thesis defense to calculate power! If an examiner asks: 'Why did you choose 100 people?', never say: 'My senior told me 100 is enough.' Say: 'We conducted an a priori power analysis in G*Power 3.1 assuming a medium effect size of 0.15, alpha 0.05, and power 0.80, which determined a minimum requirement of 92 valid responses.' The examiner will nod and move on.

questions.q: True or False: If your thesis study finds a non-significant p-value (e.g. p = 0.15), you should run a post-hoc power calculation in G*Power to explain that low statistical power caused the failure.
options: True — post-hoc power proves to examiners that the sample was simply too small.
False — post-hoc power is statistically circular and rejected by academic committees; power must be determined a priori.
questions.hint: Recall the quote from Prof. Andy Field on post-hoc power.
questions.explanation: False. Post-hoc power is mathematically redundant with the p-value. Methodologists universally reject post-hoc power analysis. Sample size must be planned a priori before data collection commences.

key: Statistical power (1 - beta = 0.80) is the likelihood of detecting a true effect when one exists.
Underpowered studies risk Type II false-negative errors (missing real relationships).
Cohen established universal effect size benchmarks: t-tests (d = 0.2, 0.5, 0.8), ANOVA (f = 0.1, 0.25, 0.4), regression (f² = 0.02, 0.15, 0.35).
G*Power 3.1 calculates that a 5-predictor regression at medium effect (f² = 0.15) requires N = 92 usable responses.
Always oversample by 20% to 30% to insulate your dataset against survey non-response and missing data.
Never compute post-hoc power; always plan sample size a priori and document the protocol in Chapter 3.
mistakes: Determining sample size by guessing or copying what an older student did without calculation.
Confusing Type I error (alpha = 0.05) with Type II error (beta = 0.20).
Distributing exactly 92 surveys when 92 are needed, resulting in an underpowered study after data screening.
Calculating post-hoc power after finding a non-significant p-value (statistically invalid).
Failing to cite G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) and Cohen (1988) in Chapter 3.
